headline: A war crimes judge wins the Peace Prize
summary: Navi Pillay, 85, won the Nobel Peace Prize for a career putting war crimes on trial: a judge at the Rwanda genocide tribunal, then UN human rights chief. She grew up a bus driver's daughter in Durban under apartheid. Israel called the award a "grotesque weaponisation". Hours later, the US sanctioned the International Criminal Court.

cover_question.q: Why did a judge win for peace?

cover_answer: She put war crimes on trial. The committee calls that peace.
table_question: Would you do a job well if the powerful hated you for it?

5-7.script: A judge named Navi Pillay won the Nobel Peace Prize today. She is 85, and her dad drove a bus in South Africa. When people did terrible things in a war, she was the judge, like a referee who stops the game and writes down the foul. She thought the phone call was a joke, and it wasn't.
5-7.why: Her dad drove a bus and she became the referee. That is the whole story at six.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old reasons from what is in front of them, so the script gives one person and a dad who drove a bus, then one picture for the work: the referee who stops the game and writes down the foul. Court and genocide stay out. Expect "what did the bad people do?" Hurt a lot of people in a war, and a judge dealt with it.

8-12.script: Navi Pillay grew up under apartheid, a bus driver's daughter. First non-white woman on South Africa's high court, then a judge at the Rwanda genocide tribunal, then the UN's human rights chief. A checklist of firsts, each a bigger court. The Nobel committee says it got war crimes prosecuted.
8-12.why: A ladder of firsts, each a bigger court.
8-12.why_long: This age is working out whether rules apply to everyone, so the script climbs her career as a ladder: a province, a country, a tribunal, the UN. A child this age notices who was kept out before. Expect "who makes countries obey a court?" Nobody can force them, and the prize says the trials matter anyway.

13-17.script: Can law work without an army? The Nobel committee gave Navi Pillay, 85, the prize for getting war crimes to trial and called law "an absolute necessity". Hours later the US sanctioned the International Criminal Court, where she once sat. Second: can a prize for law stay neutral when the law names a side?
13-17.why: A court with no army, and a government that sanctions it the same day.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: law as a necessity, in the committee's words, and this award as a weapon, in Israel's. The script gives both and asks if a prize for law can stay neutral. Expect "who is right about Gaza?" The inquiry's finding, Israel's rejection, and the committee's no position.

5-7.q: Why did a judge win for peace?
5-7.a: She made sure people who did terrible things in wars went to court. The prize people say that helps keep peace.

8-12.a: The Rwanda genocide trials. She led that court for four years.
No. She joked she'd share it if people clapped more.

13-17.q: Can law work without an army?
13-17.a: The committee says it has to: law is "an absolute necessity".

13-17.q: Why is Israel angry about it?
13-17.a: Her UN inquiry said Israel committed genocidal acts in Gaza.
